title: Capstone: netkit
sub: Build one tested, installable command that combines subnet maths, ping, DNS, port scan and log analysis
goals: Structure a Python project as an installable package with a src layout and pyproject.toml
Build a multi-command CLI with argparse subcommands and shared options
Separate parsing, networking and presentation so each piece can be tested alone
Write pytest tests for pure functions, a real loopback socket and the CLI itself
Make a tool behave in pipelines with exit codes, quiet mode, stdin and JSON or CSV output
Review your own code against a rubric

blocks.text: You will build `netkit`, one command with five subcommands: `subnet` (from [Addressing](#addressing)), `ping` (from [Reachability](#net-reach)), `dns` (from [DNS](#dns)), `scan` (from [Python for networking](#py-net) and [Ports](#ports)) and `logs` (from [Python files](#py-files) and the loganalyzer). Each one started as a shell pipeline or a script. Here they become a single package with a shared output layer, tests and an installable entry point, so that `netkit scan 127.0.0.1 -p 8000-9000 -f json | jq` just works.

This is a long build. Plan two hours, commit to git after every step ([Thinking](#thinking) covers the commands), and run the checkpoint at the end of each step before continuing. When a test fails, read the failure before you change anything.
What you are building

blocks.code:
netkit subnet|ping|dns|scan|logs  [-f table|json|csv] [-q] [-v]
                                  │
                         cli.py   │  argparse subparsers, exit codes, logging
        ┌────────────┬────────────┼────────────┬─────────────┐
        ▼            ▼            ▼            ▼             ▼
    subnet.py     ping.py     dnscheck.py    scan.py       logs.py       "doing" layer:
    ipaddress     subprocess  socket, dig    socket,       re, Counter   one module per command,
                  + regex                    threads                     no printing, no argv
        └────────────┴─────┬──────┴─────────────┴─────────────┘
                           ▼
                      models.py   (dataclasses: ScanResult, PingStats)
                           ▼
                      output.py   rows (list of dicts) ──▶ table | csv | json   "presentation" layer

blocks.text: The rule that makes this testable: **modules return data, `cli.py` prints it.** A function that calls `print()` can only be tested by capturing output. A function that returns a list of dicts can be tested with one `assert`. The only module that touches `sys.argv`, `sys.stdin`, `print` or `sys.exit` is `cli.py`.
The command contract
Write down how the tool behaves before you write it. These rules are what make a program a good citizen in [pipelines](#pipes):

head: Rule
Behavior
rows: written to **stdout**, nothing else on stdout
print nothing at all; the exit status is the answer
the command did its job and the answer is "good"
the command ran and the answer is "bad" (no open ports, packet loss, bad input line, unparsable log)
the command was used wrongly or refused (bad option, refused target, unreadable file)
`subnet` and `logs` read stdin when no argument is given

blocks.text: In zsh, `netkit ping {{host}} --max-avg 50 || echo slow` only works if the program reports failure through its exit status. `grep` set this convention (0 found, 1 not found, 2 error), and tools that follow it compose with `&&`, `||`, `if` and `set -e` without any parsing.
The package layout

blocks.code:
netkit/                       project root (a git repository)
├── pyproject.toml            name, version, dependencies, the `netkit` command
├── README.md
├── src/
│   └── netkit/               the importable package
│       ├── __init__.py       version
│       ├── __main__.py       lets you run:  python3 -m netkit
│       ├── cli.py            argparse + exit codes + logging
│       ├── models.py         dataclasses
│       ├── output.py         table / csv / json
│       ├── subnet.py  ping.py  dnscheck.py  scan.py  logs.py
└── tests/
    ├── test_subnet.py  test_ping.py  test_scan.py  test_logs.py  test_cli.py

blocks.text: The `src/` layout puts the package one level down. Tests then import the **installed** package, not whatever happens to be in the current directory, which catches missing files and wrong imports before users do.

blocks.name: netkit
blocks.sum: The command you build in this chapter: five subcommands behind one entry point.

how.text: Each subcommand is an `argparse` sub-parser that shares `-f/--format`, `-q/--quiet` and `-v/--verbose` through a parent parser. `cli.main(argv)` builds the parser, runs one function per command and returns an exit status, and `sys.exit(main())` hands that to the shell. Options for the shared group go **after** the subcommand: `netkit subnet -f json 10.0.0.0/8`.

examples.desc: Scan your own Mac and keep only the open ports as JSON
Open ports as a plain list for a loop
Top client addresses from a log, as CSV for sort or awk

blocks.text: Design decisions worth understanding
Every choice in `netkit` has a reason, and each reason applies to the next tool you write.
Rows of dicts as the common currency

Every command returns `list[dict]` with identical keys per row. A table needs column headers and aligned cells, CSV needs a header row and one value per column, and JSON needs serializable values. All three are views of the same rows, so `output.render` is 25 lines instead of five formatters. The cost is that nested data must be flattened first, which is why `logs` emits `section,key,value` rows instead of a nested dict. That shape is also friendlier to `awk`, as the pipe examples show.
Dataclasses for results, dicts for output

`ScanResult` and `PingStats` are frozen dataclasses: typed, immutable, with a free `__repr__` and `__eq__`. Tests compare them directly (`assert result == ScanResult(...)`). The `as_row()` method is the only bridge to the presentation layer. If you later add an HTML report or a database writer, you add a new consumer and leave the producers alone.
Subprocess for ping and dig, sockets for scan

Use the operating system's own tool when it does a privileged or complicated job well (`ping` needs special permission for ICMP; `dig` implements the whole DNS protocol, including TCP fallback). Use the standard library when it is simple and gives you control (a TCP connect test is four lines of `socket`). The price of a child process is parsing its text, which is why `parse_ping` is a separate, tested function, and why `dnscheck` reports a clear error when `dig` is missing.
Threads in scan, not in ping

A scan makes hundreds of independent, short, waiting operations, so a thread pool pays off at once. `ping` over several hosts could use threads as well, but a ping already waits one second per packet, and parallelism there changes the output order and the load on your network. Add it only when you measure a need.
Errors: expected versus unexpected

`cli.py` catches the exceptions it **expects** from users and the world: `ValueError` from bad input, `OSError` from missing files and refused sockets, `RuntimeError` from a missing `ping`. It turns each into one log line and an exit status. It does not catch `Exception`, because a `TypeError` or `KeyError` is a bug in your code, and the traceback is exactly what you want to see while developing. Swallowing those would hide the evidence.

`logging.basicConfig` does nothing if the root logger already has handlers. pytest installs its own handlers, so without `force=True` the error messages would never reach `capsys` and the CLI tests that check stderr would fail. The same call works in normal runs.
Working in PyCharm
Open `~/lab/netkit` as a project and choose the existing `.venv` interpreter (Settings, Project, Python Interpreter, Add Interpreter, Existing). Then:

items.text: Mark `src` as a **Sources Root** (right-click the folder, Mark Directory as) so the editor resolves `import netkit`.

Right-click `tests/` and choose Run `pytest in tests`. PyCharm lists each test and shows the failing assertion with a diff. If it offers unittest instead, set Settings, Tools, Python Integrated Tools, Default test runner, to pytest.

Create a Run configuration of type Python with **Module name** `netkit` and **Parameters** `scan 127.0.0.1 -p 8000-8003`. This runs `python -m netkit`, which is what `__main__.py` is for. Click the gutter beside a line in `scan.py` to set a breakpoint, and run that configuration with Debug.
Use the Terminal tool window for `pytest -q` and the `netkit` command; it activates `.venv` for you.

Step 2: Subnet maths, output formats and a first command
Start from the two pure modules. Both run in the page, so test them here first, then save only the part **above** the demo marker as the file named in the first line.

First `src/netkit/subnet.py`. `describe` turns text such as `192.168.1.23/26` into a dict of facts, relying on `ipaddress` as in [Addressing](#addressing). `net.hosts()` excludes network and broadcast addresses; a /31 point-to-point link (RFC 3021) has two usable addresses, a case the tests will pin down.

blocks.code:
# src/netkit/subnet.py  (save everything above the "demo" line)
"""Subnet maths on top of the standard ipaddress module."""
import ipaddress


def describe(text):
    """Return a dict describing an address with prefix, e.g. 192.168.1.23/26.

    Raises ValueError for text that is not a valid IPv4 or IPv6 interface.
    """
    iface = ipaddress.ip_interface(text)
    net = iface.network
    usable = net.num_addresses - 2 if net.version == 4 and net.prefixlen < 31 else net.num_addresses
    hosts = list(net.hosts()) if net.num_addresses <= 2**16 else []
    return {
        "address": str(iface.ip),
        "network": str(net.network_address),
        "prefix": net.prefixlen,
        "netmask": str(net.netmask),
        "broadcast": str(net.broadcast_address) if net.version == 4 else "",
        "first_host": str(hosts[0]) if hosts else "",
        "last_host": str(hosts[-1]) if hosts else "",
        "usable_hosts": usable,
        "private": net.is_private,
    }


# ---- demo: do not save below this line ----
for text in ["192.168.1.23/26", "10.0.0.0/31"]:
    d = describe(text)
    print(d["network"], d["broadcast"], d["first_host"], d["last_host"], d["usable_hosts"])
try:
    describe("300.1.1.1/24")
except ValueError as exc:
    print("ValueError:", exc)

blocks.text: Next `src/netkit/output.py`. Every command produces a **list of dicts** (rows with the same keys) and this one function turns them into a table, CSV or JSON. The table widths are computed from the data, so no column is truncated.

blocks.code:
# src/netkit/output.py  (save everything above the "demo" line)
"""Render a list of dict rows as a table, CSV or JSON."""
import csv
import io
import json


def render(rows, fmt="table"):
    """Return text for rows (a list of dicts with the same keys)."""
    if fmt == "json":
        return json.dumps(rows, indent=2)
    if not rows:
        return ""
    keys = list(rows[0])
    if fmt == "csv":
        buf = io.StringIO()
        writer = csv.DictWriter(buf, fieldnames=keys, lineterminator="\n")
        writer.writeheader()
        writer.writerows(rows)
        return buf.getvalue().rstrip("\n")
    widths = {k: max(len(k), *(len(str(r[k])) for r in rows)) for k in keys}
    head = "  ".join(k.upper().ljust(widths[k]) for k in keys)
    body = ["  ".join(str(r[k]).ljust(widths[k]) for k in keys).rstrip() for r in rows]
    return "\n".join([head.rstrip(), *body])


# ---- demo: do not save below this line ----
rows = [{"host": "192.168.1.1", "port": 22, "state": "open"},
        {"host": "192.168.1.10", "port": 8080, "state": "open"}]
print(render(rows))
print()
print(render(rows, "csv"))
print()
print(render(rows, "json"))

blocks.text: Now the first version of the CLI, `src/netkit/cli.py`. It knows one subcommand. You replace it in Step 7.

blocks.code:
"""Command-line entry point (first version: subnet only)."""
import argparse
import sys

from netkit import __version__
from netkit.output import render
from netkit.subnet import describe


def build_parser():
    p = argparse.ArgumentParser(prog="netkit", description="Small network toolkit.")
    p.add_argument("--version", action="version", version=f"netkit {__version__}")
    sub = p.add_subparsers(dest="command", required=True)
    s = sub.add_parser("subnet", help="describe CIDR networks")
    s.add_argument("cidr", nargs="+", help="e.g. 192.168.1.23/26")
    s.add_argument("-f", "--format", choices=["table", "json", "csv"], default="table")
    return p


def main(argv=None):
    args = build_parser().parse_args(argv)
    rows = [describe(c) for c in args.cidr]
    print(render(rows, args.format))
    return 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())

Step 3: ping and latency

`ping.py` runs the system `ping` as a child process and parses its summary. The parser is a separate pure function, `parse_ping`, so tests feed it saved text from both macOS and Linux and never need a network. The models go in their own file:

blocks.code:
"""Run the system ping and turn its text into numbers."""
import re
import subprocess
import sys

from netkit.models import PingStats

COUNTS_RE = re.compile(r"(\d+) packets transmitted, (\d+)(?: packets)? received")
LOSS_RE = re.compile(r"([\d.]+)% packet loss")
RTT_RE = re.compile(r"=\s*([\d.]+)/([\d.]+)/([\d.]+)")


def parse_ping(host, text):
    """Parse macOS or Linux ping output. Return PingStats, or None if no summary."""
    counts = COUNTS_RE.search(text)
    loss = LOSS_RE.search(text)
    if not counts or not loss:
        return None
    sent, received = int(counts.group(1)), int(counts.group(2))
    rtt = RTT_RE.search(text)
    lo, avg, hi = (float(x) for x in rtt.groups()) if rtt else (0.0, 0.0, 0.0)
    return PingStats(host, sent, received, float(loss.group(1)), lo, avg, hi)


def ping(host, count=4, timeout=10.0):
    """Ping host `count` times. Raises RuntimeError if ping is missing or fails to run."""
    cmd = ["ping", "-c", str(count), host]
    try:
        proc = subprocess.run(cmd, capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=timeout + count)
    except FileNotFoundError:
        raise RuntimeError("the ping command was not found") from None
    except subprocess.TimeoutExpired:
        raise RuntimeError(f"ping {host} timed out") from None
    stats = parse_ping(host, proc.stdout)
    if stats is None:
        message = (proc.stderr or proc.stdout).strip().splitlines()
        raise RuntimeError(message[-1] if message else f"no ping summary for {host}")
    return stats

blocks.text: Look at the three regular expressions. macOS prints `4 packets transmitted, 3 packets received, 25.0% packet loss`; Linux prints `4 packets transmitted, 4 received, 0% packet loss`. The `(?: packets)?` group makes the word optional. When every packet is lost there is no `round-trip` line, which the parser handles by returning zeros instead of failing.
**Checkpoint 3.** Try it directly from Python (the CLI gets the command in Step 7). Use a host you own, such as your router or `127.0.0.1`:

$ python3 -c "from netkit.ping import ping; print(ping('127.0.0.1', 3))"

blocks.title: Why a child process and not raw ICMP

blocks.text: Sending ICMP from Python needs a raw socket and root. The system `ping` is already set up to do that safely (it is setuid or uses a privileged socket), so the program calls it with a **list** of arguments, never `shell=True`, and a `timeout`.
Step 4: dns

`dnscheck.py` has two ways to resolve. With no `--server`, it uses `socket.getaddrinfo`, the same resolution path as your browser, so it includes `/etc/hosts` and VPN rules. With `--server`, it runs `dig +short @server name type` and returns the answer lines. The `compare` function asks several servers and reports whether they agree, which is the heart of the DNS-hijack check from [DNS](#dns).

`+time` and `+tries=1` keep `dig` from retrying for 15 seconds on an unreachable resolver. `sorted` makes answer order irrelevant, because DNS round-robin changes the order of records between queries and would otherwise look like a disagreement.
**Checkpoint 3b.**

blocks.code:
$ python3 -c "from netkit.dnscheck import compare; print(compare('example.com', 'A', ['1.1.1.1', '9.9.9.9']))"
([{'name': 'example.com', 'type': 'A', 'server': '1.1.1.1', 'answer': '93.184.216.34'}, {'name': 'example.com', 'type': 'A', 'server': '9.9.9.9', 'answer': '93.184.216.34'}], True)

blocks.text: Step 5: the port scanner

`scan.py` is the scanner from [Python for networking](#py-net), reorganized so that it returns `ScanResult` objects and enforces the address rule in one place (`scan` raises `PermissionError` for public addresses unless `allow_public=True`).
Differences from `portscan.py`: it reads a short banner from open ports, it returns data instead of printing, and the safety check is a named function (`is_allowed`) the tests can call.

The command-line flag `--allow-public` exists for a host you own that sits on a public address, such as your own VPS, or one you have written permission to test. Do not remove the private-address check, and do not make `--allow-public` the default. Treat it like `rm -rf`: the safe default should need no thought.

blocks.text: Step 6: log analysis

`logs.py` is the combined-format parser from [Python files](#py-files), trimmed to what the CLI needs: it returns plain data, and it takes any iterable of lines, so a file, stdin and a test list all work. It runs in the page, so try it here first.

blocks.code:
# src/netkit/logs.py  (save everything above the "demo" line)
"""Summarize a combined-format web access log."""
import re
from collections import Counter, defaultdict

LOG_RE = re.compile(
    r'^(?P<ip>\S+) \S+ \S+ \[(?P<time>[^\]]+)\] '
    r'"(?P<method>[A-Z]+) (?P<path>\S+)[^"]*" (?P<status>\d{3}) (?P<bytes>\d+|-)'
)


def parse_line(line):
    """Return a dict for one log line, or None if it does not match."""
    m = LOG_RE.match(line)
    if not m:
        return None
    rec = m.groupdict()
    rec["status"] = int(rec["status"])
    rec["bytes"] = 0 if rec["bytes"] == "-" else int(rec["bytes"])
    return rec


def summarize(lines, top=5):
    """One pass over any iterable of lines. Returns a dict of plain data."""
    clients, codes, sent = Counter(), Counter(), defaultdict(int)
    total = bad = 0
    for line in lines:
        if not line.strip():
            continue
        rec = parse_line(line)
        if rec is None:
            bad += 1
            continue
        total += 1
        clients[rec["ip"]] += 1
        codes[rec["status"]] += 1
        sent[rec["ip"]] += rec["bytes"]
    return {
        "requests": total,
        "unparsable": bad,
        "top_clients": clients.most_common(top),
        "status": sorted(codes.items()),
        "bytes_by_client": sorted(sent.items(), key=lambda kv: -kv[1])[:top],
    }


# ---- demo: do not save below this line ----
SAMPLE = [
    '203.0.113.7 - - [07/Oct/2026:09:14:08 +0000] "GET /index.html HTTP/1.1" 200 5120 "-" "curl/8.7"',
    '203.0.113.7 - - [07/Oct/2026:09:14:09 +0000] "GET /missing HTTP/1.1" 404 - "-" "curl/8.7"',
    '198.51.100.8 - - [07/Oct/2026:09:15:00 +0000] "POST /api HTTP/1.1" 500 120 "-" "x"',
    "garbage",
]
s = summarize(SAMPLE, top=2)
print(s["requests"], s["unparsable"], s["top_clients"], s["status"])

blocks.text: Save the module part as `src/netkit/logs.py`. A line that does not match is counted in `unparsable` instead of crashing the run. The function also never holds the whole file in memory, only counters, so it handles a multi-gigabyte log.
Step 7: the full command line

Replace `src/netkit/cli.py` with the finished version. Read the structure before typing it: `build_parser` declares the interface, one `cmd_*` function per subcommand does the work and returns an exit status, and `main` ties them together with logging.

blocks.code:
"""Command-line entry point: netkit subnet|ping|dns|scan|logs."""
import argparse
import logging
import sys

from netkit import __version__, dnscheck, logs, ping as pingmod, scan as scanmod, subnet
from netkit.output import render

log = logging.getLogger("netkit")

OK, FAILED, USAGE = 0, 1, 2


def build_parser():
    p = argparse.ArgumentParser(prog="netkit", description="Small network toolkit.")
    p.add_argument("--version", action="version", version=f"netkit {__version__}")
    common = argparse.ArgumentParser(add_help=False)
    common.add_argument("-f", "--format", choices=["table", "json", "csv"], default="table")
    common.add_argument("-q", "--quiet", action="store_true", help="print nothing, use the exit status")
    common.add_argument("-v", "--verbose", action="store_true", help="log details to stderr")
    sub = p.add_subparsers(dest="command", required=True)

    s = sub.add_parser("subnet", parents=[common], help="describe CIDR networks")
    s.add_argument("cidr", nargs="*", help="e.g. 192.168.1.23/26 (reads stdin when omitted)")

    s = sub.add_parser("ping", parents=[common], help="latency and loss through the system ping")
    s.add_argument("host", nargs="+")
    s.add_argument("-c", "--count", type=int, default=4)
    s.add_argument("--max-avg", type=float, metavar="MS", help="exit 1 if the average RTT exceeds MS")

    s = sub.add_parser("dns", parents=[common], help="resolve names, optionally compare servers")
    s.add_argument("name", nargs="+")
    s.add_argument("-t", "--type", default="A", help="record type for --server queries")
    s.add_argument("-s", "--server", action="append", help="resolver to ask via dig (repeatable)")

    s = sub.add_parser("scan", parents=[common], help="TCP connect scan of your own hosts")
    s.add_argument("host")
    s.add_argument("-p", "--ports", default="1-1024")
    s.add_argument("--timeout", type=float, default=0.5)
    s.add_argument("--workers", type=int, default=100)
    s.add_argument("--all", action="store_true", help="also list closed ports")
    s.add_argument("--allow-public", action="store_true",
                   help="I own this host or have written permission to test it")

    s = sub.add_parser("logs", parents=[common], help="summarize a web access log")
    s.add_argument("file", nargs="?", default="-", help="log file, or - for stdin")
    s.add_argument("--top", type=int, default=5)
    return p


def say(args, text):
    if text and not args.quiet:
        print(text)


def cmd_subnet(args):
    items = args.cidr or [ln.strip() for ln in sys.stdin if ln.strip()]
    rows, bad = [], 0
    for item in items:
        try:
            rows.append(subnet.describe(item))
        except ValueError as exc:
            log.error("%s", exc)
            bad += 1
    say(args, render(rows, args.format))
    return FAILED if bad else OK


def cmd_ping(args):
    rows, worst = [], OK
    for host in args.host:
        try:
            stats = pingmod.ping(host, args.count)
        except RuntimeError as exc:
            log.error("%s", exc)
            worst = FAILED
            continue
        rows.append(stats.as_row())
        if stats.received == 0 or (args.max_avg and stats.avg_ms > args.max_avg):
            worst = FAILED
    say(args, render(rows, args.format))
    return worst


def cmd_dns(args):
    rows, agree = [], True
    try:
        for name in args.name:
            if args.server:
                found, same = dnscheck.compare(name, args.type, args.server)
                rows += found
                agree = agree and same
            else:
                rows.append({"name": name, "type": "A/AAAA", "server": "system",
                             "answer": " ".join(dnscheck.lookup_system(name))})
    except (LookupError, RuntimeError) as exc:
        log.error("%s", exc)
        return FAILED
    say(args, render(rows, args.format))
    if not agree:
        log.warning("servers disagree")
    return OK if agree else FAILED


def cmd_scan(args):
    try:
        ports = scanmod.parse_ports(args.ports)
        results = scanmod.scan(args.host, ports, args.timeout, args.workers, args.allow_public)
    except PermissionError as exc:
        log.error("%s", exc)
        return USAGE
    except (ValueError, OSError) as exc:
        log.error("%s", exc)
        return USAGE
    shown = [r for r in results if args.all or r.state == "open"]
    if shown or args.format != "table":
        say(args, render([r.as_row() for r in shown], args.format))
    else:
        say(args, f"no open ports among {len(ports)} scanned")
    return OK if any(r.state == "open" for r in results) else FAILED


def cmd_logs(args):
    try:
        if args.file == "-":
            summary = logs.summarize(sys.stdin, args.top)
        else:
            with open(args.file, encoding="utf-8", errors="replace") as fh:
                summary = logs.summarize(fh, args.top)
    except OSError as exc:
        log.error("%s", exc)
        return USAGE
    rows = [{"section": "requests", "key": "total", "value": summary["requests"]},
            {"section": "requests", "key": "unparsable", "value": summary["unparsable"]}]
    for ip, n in summary["top_clients"]:
        rows.append({"section": "top_clients", "key": ip, "value": n})
    for code, n in summary["status"]:
        rows.append({"section": "status", "key": code, "value": n})
    for ip, n in summary["bytes_by_client"]:
        rows.append({"section": "bytes_by_client", "key": ip, "value": n})
    say(args, render(rows, args.format))
    return OK if summary["requests"] else FAILED


COMMANDS = {"subnet": cmd_subnet, "ping": cmd_ping, "dns": cmd_dns, "scan": cmd_scan, "logs": cmd_logs}


def main(argv=None):
    args = build_parser().parse_args(argv)
    logging.basicConfig(level=logging.DEBUG if args.verbose else logging.WARNING,
                        format="netkit: %(levelname)s: %(message)s", stream=sys.stderr, force=True)
    try:
        return COMMANDS[args.command](args)
    except BrokenPipeError:
        return OK
    except KeyboardInterrupt:
        return 130

blocks.text: Points to study:

items.text: `common` is a **parent parser** with `add_help=False`. Every subcommand inherits `-f`, `-q` and `-v` from it, so you declare them once.
`logging.basicConfig(..., stream=sys.stderr, force=True)` sends diagnostics to stderr. `log.error(...)` replaces the traceback you saw in Step 2.
`cmd_scan` returns `USAGE` (2) for refused targets and bad ports, `FAILED` (1) when no port is open, and `OK` (0) otherwise.
`except BrokenPipeError` handles `netkit ... | head -1`: when `head` exits early, the next `print` would raise. Returning cleanly is the correct behaviour for a filter.
`args.cidr or [... sys.stdin ...]` lets `subnet` read one CIDR per line from a pipe.

Step 8: tests

A test is a small program that fails loudly when the code is wrong. Install is already done (`.[dev]` included pytest). The tests have three flavours: pure functions with plain `assert`, the scanner against a **real loopback listener** in a thread (a socket test with no external network), and the CLI through `cli.main([...])` with `capsys` capturing output.

blocks.name: pytest.monkeypatch
blocks.sum: Temporarily replace an attribute, function or environment variable inside one test.
blocks.syntax: def test_x(monkeypatch, capsys): monkeypatch.setattr(target, value) ; monkeypatch.setenv(name, value)

how.text: `monkeypatch` is a **fixture**: pytest creates it for any test function that names it as a parameter, and undoes every change when the test ends. `capsys` is another: it captures what the code wrote to stdout and stderr, available through `capsys.readouterr()`. Replacing `sys.stdin` with `io.StringIO("...")` is how you test a command that reads a pipe.

blocks.name: pytest.mark.parametrize
blocks.sum: Run one test function once for each of several inputs.

how.text: Each value becomes its own test case with its own pass or fail line, so a failure on `"70000"` does not hide the result for `"0"`. Pass several parameter names as one comma-separated string, with a list of tuples.

blocks.text: Two details are deliberate. The subnet test uses `8.8.8.9/24` as a public example because Python (correctly) treats the documentation range `203.0.113.0/24` as private-use. And the scan test for a closed port opens a socket on port 0, reads the port the kernel chose, and closes it again, which guarantees a closed port with no guessing.

In `subnet.py` change `net.num_addresses - 2` to `net.num_addresses - 1`. Run `pytest -q` and read the output: pytest shows the assertion, both values, and the line. Fix the code, not the test. This is the whole point of the suite: the next time you touch `describe`, you will know within a second whether you broke it.
Step 9: README and release check
A README answers four questions: what is this, how do I install it, how do I use it, how do I run the tests. Write `README.md`:

blocks.code:
# netkit

Small network toolkit: subnet maths, ping, DNS, TCP port scan and web-log summary.

## Install

    python3 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
    pip install -e '.[dev]'

## Use

    netkit subnet 192.168.1.23/26
    netkit ping 192.168.1.1 -c 3 --max-avg 50
    netkit dns example.com -s 1.1.1.1 -s 9.9.9.9
    netkit scan 127.0.0.1 -p 1-10000
    netkit logs access.log --top 5 -f json

Results go to stdout, diagnostics to stderr. Exit status: 0 good, 1 bad result, 2 misuse.
`-f` selects table, json or csv; `-q` prints nothing.

## Safety

`scan` refuses addresses that are not loopback, private or link-local unless you pass
`--allow-public`. Scan only machines you own or have written permission to test.

## Test

    pytest -q

blocks.text: How to review your own code
Reading your own code a day later is a skill. Take 20 minutes, print or open each file, and score it against this rubric. Fix anything below a 2.

head: Area
rows: some commands crash on bad input
handles bad input, exit codes inconsistent
every failure path has a message and the right exit code
only `cli.py` prints, reads argv and exits
guard exists but can be skipped silently
guard default-on, bypass explicit and documented
bad input, boundaries (/31, empty log, 0 packets) and one real socket
a stranger can guess what a function does
catches the specific exception and logs why

blocks.text: Then do the cold-read test: open `cli.py` and explain aloud what `netkit logs -` does, step by step, without running it. Wherever you hesitate, the code is unclear. Add a comment or rename something. Then use a linter once: `pip install ruff && ruff check src tests` (see [Python modules](#py-modules)) and look at what it finds.
Recipe: add a subcommand
Adding `netkit hash FILE` (print the SHA-256 of a file) shows how little the structure asks of you. The same six moves apply to every follow-on project below.

items.text: **Write the pure function first**, in a new module, returning data: `def digest(path): ...` returning `{"file": path, "sha256": hexstring}`. Read the file in 64 KiB chunks with `hashlib.sha256().update(chunk)` so a large file does not fill memory.
**Test it**: create a file under pytest's `tmp_path` fixture containing `b"abc"` and assert the known digest `ba7816bf8f01cfea414140de5dae2223b00361a396177a9cb410ff61f20015ad`.
**Declare the interface** in `build_parser`: `s = sub.add_parser("hash", parents=[common], help="SHA-256 of files")` and `s.add_argument("file", nargs="+")`.
**Write `cmd_hash(args)`**: call the function for each file, collect rows, `say(args, render(rows, args.format))`, return `OK`, or `USAGE` with a `log.error` when a file cannot be read.

blocks.text: Compare your result with the system tool: `shasum -a 256 FILE` must print the same digest. If the two disagree, one of them is wrong, and `shasum` is not the one to suspect first.

Implement `hash` in 20 minutes. If step 3 raises `error: argument command: invalid choice`, you forgot to reinstall or to register the command. Use `git diff` before committing and read your own change as a reviewer would.
Follow-on projects
Each of these reuses the same ideas. Pick one, write its contract (inputs, outputs, exit codes) before any code, and add it to `netkit` as a new subcommand or as a separate tool.

head: Project
Spec
Stretch goals
rows: `netkit tail FILE --alert 'status=5\d\d' --every 10`: follow a growing file (like `tail -f`), count matches per window, print a line to stderr when the count passes a threshold
handle log rotation (inode change); send a macOS notification with `osascript -e 'display notification ...'`
`netkit watch URLS.txt --interval 30`: check each URL with `http.client`, record status and time in SQLite (`sqlite3`), print a summary of the last hour
percentile response times; mark a site down only after 3 failures; `--since 24h` report
`netkit arpwatch`: run `arp -an` every 30 seconds, keep a JSON file of known MAC addresses, print new devices and IP changes
resolve MAC vendors from an OUI table; flag one MAC claiming two IPs
`netkit dns --server` already compares resolvers. Add a watch mode that checks a list of names every few minutes against 3 resolvers and logs any disagreement
ignore CDN names that legitimately differ; compare TTLs; alert on private IPs returned for public names
serve `netkit` results over HTTP with `http.server`: `GET /subnet?cidr=10.0.0.0/8` returns JSON
input validation; allow only loopback clients; add a `/scan` that is off unless a flag is set
port the zsh `netcheck.zsh` from [Scripting](#scripting): interface up, gateway ping, DNS, internet ping, HTTP, coloured OK or FAIL, exit code
a `--json` mode; run from `launchd` every 5 minutes

task.text: In a brand-new virtual environment outside the project (`/tmp/nk-fresh`), install the project with `pip install ~/lab/netkit` (no `-e`) and run `netkit --version`. Then run `pip show -f netkit | head -20` and find where the files were copied.

blocks.title: Linux ping format

task.text: Write `parse_summary(text)` returning `(sent, received)` as ints from either macOS (`4 packets transmitted, 3 packets received, ...`) or Linux (`4 packets transmitted, 4 received, ...`) text.

why.text: An optional non-capturing group, `(?: packets)?`, absorbs the word that only one platform prints. Tests with saved text from each platform keep both formats working.

task.text: In `subnet.py` change `net.num_addresses - 2` to `net.num_addresses - 1`. Run `pytest -q`, read which tests fail and what values they report, restore the line, and run `pytest -q` again until it is green.

pytest -q

why.text: A failing test names the function, the expected value and the actual value. Fixing the code, never the test, is the discipline that makes a suite worth having. Note the BSD `sed -i ''` form on macOS.

blocks.title: Add --max-loss to ping

task.text: Add `--max-loss PCT` to the `ping` subcommand: exit status 1 when any host's `loss_pct` exceeds the value. Add a test in `tests/test_cli.py` that monkeypatches `netkit.ping.ping` to return a fixed `PingStats` with 50 percent loss and checks that `cli.main(["ping", "x", "--max-loss", "10", "-q"])` returns 1.

hints: In `cli.py`, `pingmod.ping` is looked up when called, so `monkeypatch.setattr("netkit.ping.ping", fake)` takes effect.
blocks.solution:
# cli.py, in the ping subparser:
s.add_argument("--max-loss", type=float, metavar="PCT", help="exit 1 if loss exceeds PCT")
# in cmd_ping, extend the failure test:
if stats.received == 0 or (args.max_avg and stats.avg_ms > args.max_avg) \
        or (args.max_loss is not None and stats.loss_pct > args.max_loss):
    worst = FAILED
# tests/test_cli.py
def test_ping_max_loss(monkeypatch):
    from netkit.models import PingStats
    monkeypatch.setattr("netkit.ping.ping", lambda host, count=4: PingStats("x", 4, 2, 50.0, 1.0, 2.0, 3.0))
    assert cli.main(["ping", "x", "--max-loss", "10", "-q"]) == 1

why.text: Testing the CLI without a network works by replacing the one function that touches the network. The same trick tests a DNS failure, a timeout or a flapping host, which you could never reproduce on demand with real pings.

blocks.title: Use netkit in a pipeline

task.text: Using only `netkit` and standard tools, print the three client addresses that transferred the most bytes in `~/lab/access.log`, one per line, with the byte count. Use CSV output and `awk`, `sort`, `head`.

hints: Rows with section `bytes_by_client` carry the data; columns are section, key, value.
blocks.solution: netkit logs ~/lab/access.log --top 100 -f csv | awk -F, '$1=="bytes_by_client" {print $2, $3}' | sort -k2 -nr | head -3

why.text: Machine-readable output is what lets a small tool join a pipeline. `--top 100` widens the limit so `sort` sees every client, and the CSV `section` column makes `awk` filtering a one-liner.

questions.q: Why does `cli.py` return an integer from `main()` instead of calling `sys.exit` inside each command?

options.text: Commands become easy to test by comparing the return value, and one place decides the process exit
Python requires main to return an integer

questions.why: Functions that return a status can be called from tests like any other function. `sys.exit(main())` at the entry point converts the value for the shell.

questions.q: Which of these belongs in `scan.py` rather than `cli.py`?

options.text: Opening TCP connections and returning `ScanResult` objects

questions.why: The doing layer returns data. Presentation, argument handling and logging belong to the command-line layer.

questions.q: `pip install -e .[dev]` fails in zsh with `no matches found`. What is the fix?
questions.why: `[dev]` is a glob pattern to zsh. Single quotes pass it through unchanged.

questions.q: What does exit status 1 mean in netkit's contract?

options.text: The command ran and the answer is bad (no open ports, loss above threshold, bad input line)

questions.q: Why does the CLI test replace `sys.stdin` with `io.StringIO` instead of piping real input?

options.text: The code reads `sys.stdin` as a file-like object, so a fake file exercises the same path with no shell involved

questions.why: Because pipes and files expose the same file-like interface, a `StringIO` stands in for a pipe.
